walkthroughs.body_html:
Fundamentals Of Data Structures — a core area of A-Level Computer Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Fundamentals Of Data Structures brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Fundamentals Of Data Structures.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which data structure operates on a last-in-first-out basis?
options: Queue
Stack
Hash table
Graph

mcqs.q: The advantage of a circular queue over a simple linear array queue is that it:
options: Stores items in sorted order automatically
Never becomes full
Allows items to be removed from the middle
Reuses the array space freed at the front when items are dequeued

mcqs.q: A hash table achieves fast lookup by:
options: Keeping all keys in sorted order
Searching every item in turn
Applying a hash function to the key to compute its storage index directly
Storing each item twice

mcqs.q: An in-order traversal of a binary search tree visits the items in:
options: Random order
Ascending order
The order they were inserted
Reverse insertion order

mcqs.q: Does a stack remove the item that has been waiting longest?
options: Yes - all data structures release their oldest item first.
No - a stack is LIFO: pop removes the most recently pushed item from the top; it is a queue that removes the longest-waiting item (FIFO).
Yes - all tree traversals output items in sorted order.
A stack removes a random item each time.

mcqs.q: Does a collision mean a hash table has failed?
options: Yes - a collision corrupts the table and loses one of the items.
Yes - hash functions are designed so collisions can never occur.
No - collisions, where two keys hash to the same index, are expected; techniques such as chaining or probing handle them while keeping fast average performance.
Yes - all tree traversals output items in sorted order.

mcqs.q: Does an in-order traversal of any binary tree produce sorted output?
options: Yes - all tree traversals output items in sorted order.
Yes - hash functions are designed so collisions can never occur.
Yes - in-order traversal sorts whatever tree it is applied to.
No - in-order traversal is only guaranteed to give ascending order for a binary SEARCH tree, where the left-less-than-right ordering property holds.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Binary search tree”?
options: A first-in-first-out (FIFO) structure where items join at the rear and leave from the front, like a waiting line.
A structure that applies a hash function to a key to compute a storage index, giving very fast average-case lookup, insertion and deletion.
A last-in-first-out (LIFO) structure where items are pushed onto and popped from the top; used for function calls and undo features.
A binary tree where every left descendant is less than its node and every right descendant greater, enabling efficient searching.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Queue”?
options: A first-in-first-out (FIFO) structure where items join at the rear and leave from the front, like a waiting line.
A last-in-first-out (LIFO) structure where items are pushed onto and popped from the top; used for function calls and undo features.
A structure that applies a hash function to a key to compute a storage index, giving very fast average-case lookup, insertion and deletion.
A queue implemented in an array whose rear pointer wraps around to the start, reusing the space freed by dequeued items.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Hash table”?
options: A first-in-first-out (FIFO) structure where items join at the rear and leave from the front, like a waiting line.
A structure that applies a hash function to a key to compute a storage index, giving very fast average-case lookup, insertion and deletion.
A dynamic structure of nodes, each holding data and a pointer to the next node, allowing insertion and deletion without shifting elements.
A last-in-first-out (LIFO) structure where items are pushed onto and popped from the top; used for function calls and undo features.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Linked list”?
options: A last-in-first-out (LIFO) structure where items are pushed onto and popped from the top; used for function calls and undo features.
A structure that applies a hash function to a key to compute a storage index, giving very fast average-case lookup, insertion and deletion.
A dynamic structure of nodes, each holding data and a pointer to the next node, allowing insertion and deletion without shifting elements.
A queue implemented in an array whose rear pointer wraps around to the start, reusing the space freed by dequeued items.

A structure that applies a hash function to a key to compute a storage index, giving very fast average-case lookup, insertion and deletion.
A queue implemented in an array whose rear pointer wraps around to the start, reusing the space freed by dequeued items.

A queue implemented in an array whose rear pointer wraps around to the start, reusing the space freed by dequeued items.
A binary tree where every left descendant is less than its node and every right descendant greater, enabling efficient searching.

3 items
11 items
5 items
